title: Can you find your iPhone when it's off?
caption:
Can you find an iPhone when it's off? Apple says yes, for a while.
Up to 24 hours on a supported iPhone, but only if one switch is on.
Were yours on? Yes or no?

can iphone be found when turned off
does find my iphone work when phone is off
pinned_comment: Short version: Apple's iPhone User Guide says "On a supported iPhone, turning on the Find My network allows you to locate your iPhone for up to 24 hours after it's turned off, or up to 5 hours when it's in power reserve mode." Check yours: Settings › [your name] › Find My › Find My iPhone, then turn on Find My iPhone and Find My network. Were yours on? Yes or no?

pinned_backups.reply: Apple's word is approximate: the network's devices "report their approximate location back to the owner." Apple's pages give no distance, so we don't either.
Apple's guide says "On a supported iPhone" and lists no models on that page, so the video names none. We'd rather not guess a model list Apple didn't print there.

Apple's guide gives two numbers: "up to 24 hours after it's turned off, or up to 5 hours when it's in power reserve mode." There's also a separate switch on the same screen: "Send Last Location: If your device's battery charge level becomes critically low, its location is sent to Apple automatically."

pinned_backups.if: So a thief can't just turn it off?
pinned_backups.reply: Apple's two pages don't talk about theft, so the video doesn't either. What they say is about locating your own lost iPhone: "up to 24 hours after it's turned off", on a supported iPhone, with the Find My network on.

pinned_backups.if: So strangers' phones can see where my iPhone is?
pinned_backups.reply: Apple describes it as "a crowdsourced network of over a billion Apple devices" and says: "It's all anonymous and encrypted to protect everyone's privacy." The approximate location goes "back to the owner".

pinned_backups.if: It doesn't work in my country.
pinned_backups.reply: Apple's page: "Find My availability and features might vary by country or region."
We only read Apple's iPhone pages, so the video makes no claim about other phones. Check your phone maker's own support page.

youtube_description:
Turned off? Your iPhone's still findable, for a while, if one switch is on. Apple's iPhone User Guide says: "On a supported iPhone, turning on the Find My network allows you to locate your iPhone for up to 24 hours after it's turned off, or up to 5 hours when it's in power reserve mode."

How? Apple says the Find My network is "a crowdsourced network of over a billion Apple devices that use Bluetooth technology to detect the location of an accessory or device, and report their approximate location back to the owner. It's all anonymous and encrypted to protect everyone's privacy." So a switched-off iPhone with no Wi-Fi and no cellular can still be spotted by Bluetooth, and its approximate location goes back to the owner.

The catch is one switch. Apple: "To make sure that you can find your devices even if they're powered off or disconnected, check that you turned on Find My network."

Check yours (about 10 seconds): Settings › [your name] › Find My › Find My iPhone. Turn on Find My iPhone and Find My network. Apple's steps: "Tap Find My iPhone, then turn on Find My iPhone." And first: "Before you can use the Find My app to locate a lost iPhone, you need to connect the device to your Apple Account."

Same screen, separate switch: "Send Last Location: If your device's battery charge level becomes critically low, its location is sent to Apple automatically."

What Apple doesn't say: the guide says "supported iPhone" and lists no models on that page, so this video names none. The location is approximate; Apple gives no distance. Every number is "up to". And "Find My availability and features might vary by country or region."

Fine print: This video is about finding your own iPhone, using Apple's two pages below. The power-off screen, the search bar, the Apple guide card and the Settings screen are re-created by hand from Apple's wording; the phone and the helper devices are generic drawings, and the city of lit windows is our illustration of "over a billion Apple devices", not a map. Not affiliated with Apple.

- Apple iPhone User Guide, "Add your iPhone to Find My" (no published date on the page), read Nov 24, 2026: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/add-your-iphone-iph9a847efc7/ios
- Apple Support, "How to turn on Find My on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac" (102648, published September 14, 2026), read Nov 24, 2026: https://support.apple.com/en-us/102648
